questions.question: What does it mean that strings are immutable in Go?
questions.title: String immutability in Go
questions.direct_answer: A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes: after a string value is created, its bytes cannot be changed through that value. Indexing returns one byte but cannot be assigned to or addressed. Code creates a new string for a changed result, often by converting to `[]byte` for byte-oriented data or `[]rune` for Unicode code-point edits, then converting back.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether immutability is separated from variable reassignment, UTF-8 validity, and compiler allocation choices.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to assign to a string index or assuming every indexed byte is one complete character.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why byte and rune transformations serve different kinds of input.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A string stores a fixed sequence of bytes.
`s[i]` reads one byte but cannot appear on the left of an assignment.
A string may contain arbitrary bytes, not only valid UTF-8.
Build a changed value instead of mutating the original.
Choose bytes or runes according to the data being changed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes. `len(s)` reports the number of bytes, and `s[i]` reads the byte at one index, but code cannot assign to `s[i]` or take its address. Assigning a new string to the variable is allowed because that replaces the variable's value; it does not modify the old string.

Immutability makes string values safe to share as values and suitable for map keys. It does not guarantee that the bytes are valid UTF-8. Source string literals are UTF-8, but a string created from network or file bytes may contain any byte sequence, so Unicode-sensitive code should validate when the boundary requires valid text.

For example, converting `"go"` to `[]byte`, changing the first byte, and converting back creates `"Go"` while the original remains `"go"`. For non-ASCII text, editing a byte can break an encoding, so converting to `[]rune` is safer when the operation is defined on Unicode code points.

Immutability is a semantic rule rather than a promise about one internal allocation. The compiler may optimize conversions when no observable mutation is possible, but the program must behave as if the resulting string never changes. I treat strings as text or immutable bytes and create explicit new values for transformations.

sections.title: The variable may change; the string value does not
sections.content:
A variable is a storage location that can be assigned repeatedly. A string value is the byte sequence held on one assignment. `name = strings.ToUpper(name)` points the variable at a newly produced value; it does not edit the previous sequence in place.

This distinction prevents aliases from observing hidden string mutation. Mutable work belongs in a byte slice, rune slice, builder, or another buffer whose ownership is explicit. Conversion back to string establishes the immutable result expected by string APIs.

sections.title: Transform instead of mutating
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[original immutable string] --> B[convert to bytes or runes]
  B --> C[modify owned mutable data]
  C --> D[convert to new string]
  A -. remains unchanged .-> E[original readers]
```

sections.title: Create a changed string through owned bytes
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    original := "go"
    changed := []byte(original)
    changed[0] = 'G'
    result := string(changed)
    fmt.Println(original, result)
}
```
The output is `go Go`. Mutating the byte slice does not change the original string value.

questions.question: How do you safely modify text stored in a Go string?
questions.title: Changing strings with bytes or runes
questions.direct_answer: Create a mutable representation, change it, and build a new string. Use `[]byte` when positions and replacements are defined in encoded bytes, such as ASCII protocol data; use `[]rune` when they are defined in Unicode code points. Neither automatically understands user-perceived grapheme clusters, so text-editor-style operations may need a Unicode segmentation library.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses bytes, code points, or grapheme clusters from the actual text requirement.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a byte index as a character index or claiming a rune always equals one visible character.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the grapheme-cluster boundary without overcomplicating ordinary code-point work.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Convert to `[]byte` for byte-oriented or known ASCII changes.
Convert to `[]rune` for Unicode code-point changes.
Convert the modified slice back to a new string.
A rune is not always one user-perceived character.
Validate UTF-8 when malformed external input is not allowed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Strings cannot be edited directly, so the first step is to decide what one editable unit means. If the data is an ASCII identifier or binary protocol field, bytes are the correct units. If the operation replaces Unicode code points, `[]rune` prevents a multi-byte UTF-8 encoding from being split accidentally.

For example, the word `"café"` contains five bytes but four runes. Changing byte index three would touch only part of `é`, while `runes[3] = 'e'` replaces the complete code point and produces `"cafe"`. The rune conversion decodes the string, and converting back encodes the result as UTF-8.

Code-point safety is not the same as full human-language safety. A visible symbol may contain a base rune plus combining marks, or several runes joined into one emoji. Reversing or slicing runes can separate those units. Applications that edit user-perceived characters need grapheme segmentation and often normalization rules beyond the standard conversion.

Conversions create a clear mutable ownership boundary. For many replacements, standard functions such as `strings.ReplaceAll`, `strings.Map`, or `strings.ToUpper` express the operation directly and avoid manual indexing. I choose the highest-level operation that matches the text rule, then use bytes or runes only when index-level control is required.

sections.title: Concept guide · Changing strings with bytes or runes
sections.content:
The same visual text can be viewed as encoded bytes, Unicode code points, or grapheme clusters. Each layer answers a different question. Network framing often needs bytes. Case mapping and code-point filtering operate above bytes. Cursor movement in a text editor needs grapheme boundaries.

Go's built-in string and rune tools cover the first two layers. They intentionally do not promise locale-aware words or user-perceived characters. Naming the layer prevents an algorithm that appears correct on ASCII from corrupting wider input.

sections.title: Pick the transformation unit
sections.content:
| Unit | Go representation | Good for | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encoded byte | `[]byte` | ASCII, protocols, raw data | Can split UTF-8 |
| Unicode code point | `[]rune` | Code-point replacement/filtering | Can split grapheme clusters |
| Grapheme cluster | External segmentation | Visible editing operations | Locale and normalization still matter |

sections.title: Replace one Unicode code point
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    text := "café"
    runes := []rune(text)
    runes[3] = 'e'
    fmt.Println(text, string(runes))
}
```
The output is `café cafe`. The original stays unchanged and the multi-byte `é` is replaced as one rune.

questions.question: Why can repeated string concatenation be inefficient in Go?
questions.title: Efficient string construction
questions.direct_answer: Because strings are immutable, each growing result from `result += part` may require allocating storage and copying all bytes accumulated so far. In a loop this can create repeated work. Use `strings.Builder` for text-only construction, `bytes.Buffer` when byte-oriented APIs are involved, or `strings.Join` when all pieces already exist. Simple concatenation remains clearest for a few fixed parts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether construction strategy follows input shape rather than a blanket ban on string concatenation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Replacing every small `+` expression with a Builder or copying a Builder after it has been used.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cumulative copying and distinguish `Builder`, `Join`, and `bytes.Buffer`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A growing immutable result may be allocated and copied repeatedly.
Use `strings.Join` when the pieces are already collected.
Use `bytes.Buffer` when byte slices or I/O methods shape the work.
Keep `+` for small fixed expressions where clarity wins.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Concatenating a few fixed strings is normal and readable. The concern appears when a loop repeatedly grows one immutable result. Each new result must contain all previous bytes plus the new part, so the program may allocate and copy an increasing prefix many times. Compilers can optimize some expressions, but code should not depend on eliminating an unbounded growth pattern.

`strings.Builder` owns a mutable byte buffer behind a string-focused API. Its zero value is ready to use, `WriteString` and `WriteRune` append content, and `String` produces the accumulated text. If the approximate final size is known, `Grow` can reduce reallocations. A non-zero Builder must not be copied because copies could share internal state incorrectly.

For example, building comma-separated labels in a loop can write the separator only after the first item and then append each label. If the labels already live in a slice, `strings.Join(labels, ",")` is even simpler and should usually be preferred.

`bytes.Buffer` is useful when the same construction participates in `io.Writer` or byte APIs. Benchmarks decide performance-sensitive cases, but the semantic choice is straightforward: fixed small expression uses `+`; known pieces use `Join`; incremental text uses `Builder`; incremental bytes use `Buffer`.

sections.title: Match construction to how pieces arrive
sections.content:
The cost problem is cumulative copying, not the plus operator by itself. A compiler can combine simple expressions efficiently. A loop whose final size grows with input needs one owner that can reuse capacity.

Builders and buffers provide that owner. They also make the mutation phase local: callers receive the final immutable string after construction rather than sharing a writable representation. Never copy a Builder after writing has begun; pass its pointer when helper functions must contribute.

sections.title: Choose a string construction tool
sections.content:
| Input shape | Clear tool | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Two or three fixed parts | `+` | Direct and readable |
| Existing slice of parts | `strings.Join` | Separator handling is built in |
| Parts arrive incrementally | `strings.Builder` | Reuses growing text storage |
| Byte and `io.Writer` workflow | `bytes.Buffer` | Works naturally with byte APIs |

sections.title: Build text incrementally without repeated prefixes
